column9: What is a karyotype?
column14: A chart that traces one trait through a family
column15: A grid that predicts the offspring of a cross
column16: A list of every gene found on one chromosome
column17: A picture of all of a cell's chromosomes, sorted into matching pairs
column28: A karyotype is an arrangement of a cell's chromosome pairs, numbered from largest to smallest. A chart through a family is a pedigree, and a grid of offspring is a Punnett square.
column29: Karyo- means nucleus. What would you see if you lined up everything in the nucleus?

column9: How many chromosomes are in a normal human karyotype?
column28: A normal human karyotype has 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes = 46 chromosomes.
column29: Chromosomes come in pairs, one from each parent. Count every chromosome, not every pair.

column9: In a human karyotype, the chromosome pairs that are the same in males and females are called:
column14: Sex chromosomes
column15: Autosomes
column16: Gametes
column17: Haploid chromosomes
column28: Autosomes are every pair except the sex chromosomes (XX or XY). Gametes are egg and sperm cells, and haploid means a cell has only one of each chromosome.
column29: Which chromosomes do NOT decide whether a person is male or female?

column9: How many pairs of autosomes does a human have?
column28: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus 1 pair of sex chromosomes, for 23 pairs total. 44 is the number of autosomes (22 × 2), not pairs.
column29: 23 pairs total, and one of those pairs is the sex chromosomes.

column9: In a karyotype, the sex chromosomes are the largest pair.
column28: False. The sex chromosomes are placed last, as pair 23, no matter their size. The X is fairly large, but the Y is one of the smallest chromosomes. Pair 1 is the largest.
column29: Think about where the sex chromosomes go, and how big the Y chromosome is.

column9: A karyotype shows that the person's sex chromosomes are XX. What is the person's biological sex?
column14: Female
column15: Male
column16: Male with Klinefelter syndrome
column17: Female with Turner syndrome
column28: XX = female and XY = male. Klinefelter syndrome is XXY, and Turner syndrome has only one X, so neither fits two X chromosomes and no Y.
column29: Is there a Y chromosome?

column9: Having three copies of a chromosome instead of two is called a ___.
column28: Tri- means three, so a trisomy means a cell has three copies of one chromosome instead of the usual two.
column29: Start with the prefix that means three, as in tricycle.

column9: Having only one copy of a chromosome instead of a pair is called ___.
column28: Mono- means one, so a monosomy means a cell has only one copy of a chromosome instead of two. Turner syndrome (X0) is a monosomy of the sex chromosomes.
column29: Start with the prefix that means one, as in monorail.

column9: Down syndrome is caused by which chromosome change?
column14: Trisomy 21
column15: Monosomy 21
column16: Trisomy 18
column17: An extra X chromosome
column28: Down syndrome is trisomy 21: three copies of chromosome 21. Trisomy 18 is Edwards syndrome, and an extra X in a male is Klinefelter syndrome.
column29: Look back at the disorder list. Which chromosome number goes with Down syndrome, and does it have an extra copy or a missing one?

column9: Match each disorder to its chromosome change.
column14: Turner syndrome :: A female with only one X (X0)
column15: Klinefelter syndrome :: A male with an extra X (XXY)
column16: Edwards syndrome :: Trisomy 18
column17: Patau syndrome :: Trisomy 13
column18: Cri-du-chat syndrome :: Part of chromosome 5 is missing
column28: Turner = missing X in a female (X0 instead of XX). Klinefelter = extra X in a male (XXY). Edwards = trisomy 18. Patau = trisomy 13. Cri-du-chat = deletion of part of chromosome 5.
column29: Two disorders involve the sex chromosomes, two are trisomies, and one is a missing piece.

column9: How do doctors get chromosomes to make a karyotype?
column14: From mature red blood cells
column15: From a strand of hair with no root
column16: From cells in blood or amniotic fluid
column17: From an ultrasound image of the baby
column28: The chromosomes come from cells that have a nucleus, which doctors get by drawing blood (the white blood cells) or by taking amniotic fluid (the fluid around a baby before birth). Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, a hair with no root has no living cells, and an ultrasound makes a picture of the body, not of chromosomes.
column29: You need living cells that have a nucleus.

column9: Before the chromosomes are arranged into a karyotype, they are stained. Why?
column14: The stain gives each chromosome its own pattern of bands
column15: The stain makes the chromosomes divide faster
column16: The stain turns autosomes into sex chromosomes
column17: The stain removes any extra chromosomes
column28: Chromosomes absorb the stain and show different light and dark banding patterns. Matching chromosomes have the same bands, which helps pair them up.
column29: How could you tell two chromosomes of the same size apart?

column9: Ava is designing a karyotype for a person who has one extra copy of chromosome 8. Where should she place the extra chromosome?
column14: In a new spot at the end of the karyotype
column15: In pair 1's spot, since extra chromosomes go first
column16: Nowhere, because it has no partner to pair with
column17: In pair 8's spot, next to the other two copies
column28: Every chromosome goes in the spot for its number, so the extra chromosome 8 sits with the other two copies. Seeing three in one spot is how the karyotype shows the change. An extra chromosome doesn't get a new spot or move to the front, and leaving it out would hide the problem.
column29: Each chromosome is placed by its number. Does an extra copy change which number it is?

column9: The X and Y chromosomes, which determine whether a person is male or female, are called the ___ chromosomes.
column28: X and Y are called the sex chromosomes because they decide whether a person is male or female.
column29: What does XX versus XY tell you about a person? These chromosomes are named for that.

column9: Put these chromosomes in the order they appear in a human karyotype.
column14: Chromosome 13
column15: Chromosome 1
column16: Chromosome 21
column17: Chromosome 5
column28: Autosomes are numbered from largest (pair 1) to smallest and placed in number order. The X and Y always go last, as pair 23.
column29: What does a pair's number tell you about its size? Then think about where the X and Y belong.

column9: What is nondisjunction?
column14: When chromosomes fail to separate properly during meiosis
column15: When homologous chromosomes swap pieces of DNA
column16: When a cell divides without copying its DNA first
column17: When cancer cells spread to new parts of the body
column28: Nondisjunction means 'not coming apart': a pair of chromosomes (or sister chromatids) fails to separate in meiosis. Swapping pieces is crossing over, and cancer spreading is metastasis.
column29: Dis-junction means coming apart. Non- means not.

column9: A karyotype shows 22 pairs of autosomes that all look normal. The sex chromosomes are one X and one Y. Who does it belong to?
column14: A typical female
column15: A typical male
column16: A male with Klinefelter syndrome
column17: A female with Turner syndrome
column28: 22 normal autosome pairs plus one X and one Y = 46 chromosomes, a typical male. A sex chromosome disorder would show an extra or a missing sex chromosome, and a female would have no Y.
column29: Count the sex chromosomes and look for a Y.

column9: A karyotype shows three copies of chromosome 21. The sex chromosomes are XX. Who does it belong to?
column14: A male with Down syndrome
column15: A female with Edwards syndrome
column16: A female with Turner syndrome
column17: A female with Down syndrome
column28: Three copies of chromosome 21 is trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), and XX means female. Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18, and XX is a complete pair, so there is no sex chromosome disorder.
column29: Read two things: which chromosome has an extra copy, and what the sex chromosomes are.

column9: A karyotype shows 22 normal pairs of autosomes, but only one sex chromosome: a single X. Who does it belong to?
column14: A female with Turner syndrome
column15: A typical female
column16: A male with Turner syndrome
column17: A male with Klinefelter syndrome
column28: One X and no second sex chromosome (X0) is Turner syndrome. With no Y, the person is female, and with only one sex chromosome, this is not a typical female.
column29: Is there a Y? How many sex chromosomes should a person have?

column9: A karyotype shows 22 normal pairs of autosomes, plus two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome. Who does it belong to?
column14: A typical male
column15: A female with Klinefelter syndrome
column16: A typical female
column17: A male with Klinefelter syndrome
column28: XXY is Klinefelter syndrome: an extra X in a male. The Y makes the person male, and the extra X means this is not a typical male.
column29: Is there a Y? Is the number of X chromosomes normal?

column9: A baby has three copies of chromosome 18 and no other chromosome changes. How many chromosomes are in each of the baby's body cells?
column28: A normal body cell has 46. One extra copy of chromosome 18 makes 46 + 1 = 47.
column29: Start with the normal number and add the extra copy.

column9: Jada is counting the chromosomes in a karyotype. She finds 22 pairs of autosomes and a single X, with no other sex chromosome. How many chromosomes are there in all?
column28: 22 pairs of autosomes = 44 chromosomes. Add the one X: 44 + 1 = 45. That is one fewer than the normal 46.
column29: Turn the pairs into a number of chromosomes first, then add the sex chromosome.

column9: How many autosomes are in a normal human sperm cell?
column28: A sperm cell is haploid, with 23 chromosomes: one of each pair. That is 22 autosomes + 1 sex chromosome (X or Y).
column29: A gamete gets one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs. How many of those pairs are autosomes?

column9: When building a karyotype, which features are used to match up the two chromosomes of each pair? Select all that apply.
column14: Which parent it came from
column15: Its banding pattern
column16: Its size (length)
column17: Where it was in the photo before sorting
column28: Homologous chromosomes match in size, banding pattern, and centromere position. A chromosome's spot in the photo is random, and the two chromosomes of a pair always come from different parents (one from each), so neither one can be used to match them.
column29: Look for features you can actually see when you compare two chromosomes side by side.

column9: A person's sex chromosomes are X, X, and Y. Why is this person male even though they have two X's?
column14: They have more chromosomes than a typical female has
column15: Two X chromosomes always make a person male
column16: They have a Y chromosome, and the Y makes a person male
column17: The extra X chromosome acts like a Y chromosome
column28: Having a Y chromosome makes a person male, even with an extra X. An extra X does not act like a Y, having more chromosomes does not decide sex, and two X's with no Y make a female. Anyone with a Y is male; anyone without one is female.
column29: Which chromosome do all males have?

column9: Why might doctors make a karyotype for a baby before it is born?
column14: To remove any extra chromosomes before birth
column15: To choose whether the baby will be a boy or a girl
column16: To look for extra or missing chromosomes
column17: To measure how fast the baby is growing
column28: A karyotype is a picture of the baby's chromosomes, so it can show an extra or missing chromosome before birth. It can't change anything, so it can't remove a chromosome or choose the baby's sex, and it doesn't measure growth.
column29: What can you actually see in a picture of chromosomes?

column9: Which parent's gamete decides whether a baby will be a boy or a girl?
column14: The father's sperm, because it can carry an X or a Y
column15: The mother's egg, because it can carry an X or a Y
column16: Both parents equally, because both can give a Y
column17: Neither one; the autosomes decide the baby's sex
column28: A mother is XX, so every egg carries an X. A father is XY, so half his sperm carry X (girl) and half carry Y (boy). The sperm decides.
column29: Which parent has a Y chromosome to give?

column9: In a karyotype, the largest pair of autosomes is numbered pair 1.
column28: True. The autosomes are numbered from largest (pair 1) to smallest, and the sex chromosomes go last.
column29: Think about how the autosome pairs are ordered in a karyotype.

column9: A karyotype shows 2n − 1 chromosomes. What does this mean?
column14: One chromosome has an extra copy
column15: One chromosome of a pair is missing
column16: Every chromosome is missing its partner
column17: The person has one extra set of chromosomes
column28: 2n is the normal diploid number. 2n − 1 means one chromosome is missing from one pair (a monosomy). An extra copy would be 2n + 1, and missing every partner would make the cell haploid (n).
column29: 2n is normal. What does subtracting 1 do?

column9: During meiosis, one pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate. What kinds of gametes can this make?
column14: Gametes with exactly the normal number of chromosomes
column15: Some gametes with an extra chromosome and some missing one
column16: Gametes that are diploid for every chromosome
column17: Gametes that have no chromosomes at all
column28: If a pair doesn't separate, both chromosomes go to one cell. That side ends up with an extra chromosome (n + 1) and the other side is missing one (n − 1). After fertilization, these make a trisomy or a monosomy.
column29: If both chromosomes of a pair go to the same side, what is left for the other side?

column9: If a karyotype has exactly 46 chromosomes, the person cannot have any chromosome disorder.
column28: False. The count can be normal while a chromosome is still changed. For example, part of one chromosome can be missing (a deletion), and the total is still 46.
column29: Can something be wrong with a chromosome's structure even if the count is right?

column9: A couple has had trouble having children. Why might a doctor order a karyotype for each parent?
column14: To see which parent has stronger chromosomes
column15: To measure each parent's hormone levels
column16: To count how many eggs or sperm each parent makes
column17: To look for a chromosome change that affects gametes
column28: A karyotype can show a chromosome change in a parent, like an extra X or a broken chromosome, that can lower fertility or lead to gametes with the wrong number of chromosomes. No chromosomes are 'stronger' than others, and hormone levels and egg or sperm counts are checked with other tests.
column29: Which of these could you actually see by looking at a parent's chromosomes?

column9: Nondisjunction can happen during meiosis in either the mother or the father.
column28: True. Both parents make gametes by meiosis, so an egg or a sperm can end up with an extra or missing chromosome.
column29: Do both parents make their gametes by meiosis?

column9: Which statements about autosomes are true? Select all that apply.
column14: They decide whether a person is male or female
column15: Males and females have the same 22 pairs
column16: A trisomy can happen in an autosome
column17: They are found only in sperm and egg cells
column18: They carry genes for most traits, like eye color
column28: Everyone has the same 22 pairs of autosomes, and they carry the genes for most traits. Trisomies can happen in autosomes (trisomy 21, 18, 13). The sex chromosomes, not the autosomes, decide sex, and autosomes are in every cell with a nucleus.
column29: Autosomes are everything except the X and Y.

column9: Karyotypes can be written as the total number of chromosomes, then the sex chromosomes, then any extra chromosome (for example, +21). Match each karyotype to the person it describes.
column14: 46, XX :: A typical female
column15: 46, XY :: A typical male
column16: 47, XXY :: A male with Klinefelter syndrome
column17: 45, X :: A female with Turner syndrome
column18: 47, XX, +21 :: A female with Down syndrome
column28: 46, XX and 46, XY are typical. 47, XXY has an extra X with a Y (Klinefelter, male). 45, X has only one X (Turner, female). 47, XX, +21 has an extra chromosome 21 (Down syndrome) in a female.
column29: First read the sex chromosomes, then look for a +number or a missing chromosome.

column9: Because of nondisjunction, an egg cell has 24 chromosomes instead of 23. A normal sperm fertilizes it. How many chromosomes will the zygote have?
column28: Zygote = egg + sperm = 24 + 23 = 47, so the zygote has a trisomy.
column29: Add the chromosomes from both gametes. How many does a normal sperm have?

column9: Nondisjunction makes an egg cell with no sex chromosome at all (22 autosomes only). A normal sperm carrying an X fertilizes it. What will the child have?
column14: Klinefelter syndrome (XXY), and the child will be male
column15: Down syndrome, and the child will be female
column16: Turner syndrome (X0), and the child will be female
column17: A typical karyotype, and the child will be male
column28: Egg (no sex chromosome) + sperm (X) = one X only, written X0. That is Turner syndrome. With no Y, the child is female.
column29: Add up the sex chromosomes from the egg and the sperm.

column9: Nondisjunction in Meiosis I makes a sperm cell that carries both an X and a Y. It fertilizes a normal egg (X). What will the child have?
column14: Turner syndrome (X0), and the child will be female
column15: Klinefelter syndrome (XXY), and the child will be male
column16: Down syndrome, and the child will be male
column17: A typical karyotype, and the child will be female
column28: Sperm (X and Y) + egg (X) = XXY, Klinefelter syndrome. The Y makes the child male.
column29: Add up the sex chromosomes from the egg and the sperm.

column9: A genetic counselor shows parents a karyotype of their unborn child. It has three copies of chromosome 21. What most likely caused the extra chromosome?
column14: Crossing over swapped chromosome 21 with chromosome 22
column15: The baby's cells copied chromosome 21 twice during interphase
column16: Nondisjunction in meiosis gave one parent's gamete an extra chromosome 21
column17: The father's sperm was missing chromosome 21
column28: If chromosome 21 fails to separate in a parent's meiosis, one gamete gets two copies. When it joins a normal gamete (one copy), the zygote has three: trisomy 21 (Down syndrome). A missing 21 would make a monosomy, not a trisomy.
column29: Three copies = two from one parent + one from the other. How did one gamete get two?

column9: Which of these can a karyotype show? Select all that apply.
column14: The person's biological sex
column15: Which parent each chromosome came from
column16: An extra or missing chromosome
column17: Whether the person has the flu
column18: A large piece missing from a chromosome
column28: A karyotype shows the number, size, and banding of whole chromosomes, so it reveals sex (XX or XY), an extra or missing chromosome, and a large missing piece. The two chromosomes of a pair look alike, so it can't tell which one came from the mother and which from the father, and the flu is an infection, not a chromosome change.
column29: A karyotype is a picture of whole chromosomes. Which choices could you see in that picture?

column9: For her genetic disorder project, Maya picked sickle cell disease, which is caused by a change (mutation) in one gene. Which visual should she include?
column14: A karyotype, because it shows which chromosomes are extra
column15: A karyotype, because it shows each gene as its own band
column16: A Punnett square or pedigree, since one gene is too small to see
column17: A Punnett square or pedigree, because sickle cell is a trisomy
column28: A karyotype shows whole chromosomes, so it is used for chromosome disorders. Sickle cell is caused by a change in one gene, which is far too small to see, so it is shown with a Punnett square or pedigree. Sickle cell is not a trisomy, no chromosome is extra, and each band holds many genes, not one.
column29: Chromosomal disorder → karyotype. Gene mutation → which tools?

column9: Karyotypes are made from cells that were stopped in metaphase of mitosis. Why metaphase?
column14: The DNA is loose chromatin, so it soaks up more stain
column15: The homologous pairs have already crossed over
column16: The cell has just split into two daughter cells
column17: The chromosomes are tightly coiled and easiest to see
column28: In metaphase the DNA is coiled into thick, visible chromosomes (copied, X-shaped) that are easy to photograph and pair up. In interphase it is loose chromatin and can't be seen clearly. Crossing over only happens in meiosis.
column29: Think back to mitosis: what happens to loose chromatin as the cell gets ready to divide?

column9: A karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with an X and a Y. One copy of chromosome 5 is shorter than its partner because a piece is missing. What does it show?
column14: A male with cri-du-chat syndrome
column15: A female with cri-du-chat syndrome
column16: A male with Turner syndrome
column17: A typical male with no disorder
column28: A missing piece of chromosome 5 is cri-du-chat syndrome, even though the count is a normal 46. XY means male. Turner syndrome involves a missing X, not chromosome 5.
column29: The count is normal, but look at the structure of chromosome 5. Then read the sex chromosomes.

column9: A karyotype is written as 47, XX, +13. What does it show?
column14: A male with Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)
column15: A female with Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18)
column16: A female who is missing chromosome 13
column17: A female with Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)
column28: 47 total, XX = female, +13 = an extra chromosome 13. Trisomy 13 is Patau syndrome. Edwards is trisomy 18, and a missing 13 would make 45, not 47.
column29: Read it piece by piece: total, sex chromosomes, then the extra chromosome.

column9: Nondisjunction happened while just one of a parent's gametes was being made, yet the child has the extra chromosome in every cell of their body. Why?
column14: Nondisjunction keeps happening in every one of the child's cells
column15: The extra chromosome was in the zygote, and mitosis copied it into every new cell
column16: The extra chromosome spreads from cell to cell like a virus
column17: Only the child's gametes have it, but it looks like every cell does
column28: The zygote got the extra chromosome from the gamete. Every cell in the body comes from the zygote by mitosis, which copies all chromosomes exactly, so every cell has the extra one.
column29: Every cell in your body came from one cell. How were they made?

column9: A trisomy can happen in an autosome or in the sex chromosomes. Which karyotypes show a trisomy of the **sex chromosomes**? Select all that apply.
column16: 47, XXX
column17: 47, XXY
column28: 47, XXX and 47, XXY each have three sex chromosomes, so both are sex chromosome trisomies. In 47, XX, +18 and 47, XY, +21 the extra chromosome is an autosome, and 45, X is missing a sex chromosome (a monosomy).
column29: Look only at the letters for the sex chromosomes. How many should a person have?

column9: The Lee family has three daughters. What is the chance that their next baby will be a boy?
column14: 100%, because the family is due for a boy
column15: 25%, because they already have three girls
column16: 50%, because each child's sex is decided separately by the sperm
column17: 0%, because the father must only make X sperm
column28: Each pregnancy is a new event. The father makes about half X sperm and half Y sperm, so every baby has a 50% chance of being a boy, no matter how many girls came before.
column29: Make a Punnett square for XX × XY. Does it change after each child?

column9: Isaac is building a karyotype from cut-out chromosomes. He has placed 22 matching pairs. Two chromosomes are left: one medium-large and one very small, and they don't match. What should he conclude?
column14: They are an X and a Y, so the person is male
column15: They are an autosome pair that he cut out wrong
column16: One chromosome is missing, so the person has monosomy
column17: They are two X chromosomes, so the person is female
column28: The last pair is the sex chromosomes. The X is medium-large and the Y is very small, so an unmatched large-and-small pair is XY: a typical male. Two X's would match each other in size and bands.
column29: Which pair is the only one where the two chromosomes are allowed to look different?

column9: Put the steps for making a karyotype in order.
column14: Stain the chromosomes so their bands show
column15: Arrange the pairs by number, with the sex chromosomes last
column16: Photograph the chromosomes under a microscope
column17: Collect cells from a blood sample or amniotic fluid
column18: Count the chromosomes and look for extra or missing ones
column19: Cut out the chromosomes and match the homologous pairs
column28: Get cells (blood or amniotic fluid), stain the chromosomes, photograph them, cut out and pair them, arrange them largest to smallest with the sex chromosomes last, and then analyze the count and structure.
column29: You need the cells first and the finished arrangement last, before you can analyze it.

column9: A karyotype has 47 chromosomes. Which conditions could it show? Select all that apply.
column14: Down syndrome
column15: Klinefelter syndrome
column16: Turner syndrome
column17: Edwards syndrome
column28: 47 means one extra chromosome: Down syndrome (+21), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY), and Edwards syndrome (+18) all have 47. Turner syndrome has 45 (one X missing), and cri-du-chat has 46 with part of chromosome 5 missing.
column29: 47 = one extra chromosome. Which conditions are an extra copy of something?
